claim: The majority of DNA damage response genes are up-regulated during axolotl limb regeneration based on RNAseq and microarray datasets.
source: We analyzed 190 genes associated with DDR and DNA repair from both datasets (Supplementary file 1). We found expression of DDR-related genes to be mostly up-regulated during regeneration (Figure 1a, Green).
evidence: Supported by analysis of published RNAseq and microarray data showing gene expression patterns, and validated by qPCR for 17 genes with 11 (65%) showing up-regulation.

claim: DNA damage response is evident as early as the early-bud blastema (~5 dpa) and peaks at the late-bud blastema (~14 dpa) during axolotl limb regeneration.
source: Overall, our transcriptomic and qPCR analysis of DNA repair/damage genes revealed that DDR was evident as early as the early-bud blastema (~5 dpa) and peaked at the late-bud blastema (~14 dpa).
evidence: Based on transcriptomic analysis and qPCR validation showing temporal expression patterns of DDR genes.

claim: There is no difference in DNA damage levels between intact and 14 dpa blastema cells in axolotls.
source: To associate this response with the levels of actual DNA damage, we performed alkaline single cell gel electrophoresis (comet assay) and found that there are no differences between intact and 14 dpa blastema cells, whereas cells treated with UV showed more DNA damage (Figure 1c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Demonstrated by comet assay showing no statistical difference in DNA damage between intact and blastema cells, with UV-treated cells serving as positive control.

claim: Axolotl H2AX has a conserved carboxyl tail containing the S139 and Y142 residues.
source: We found that axolotl H2AX has a conserved carboxyl tail containing the S139, also known as γ-H2AX when phosphorylated, and Y142 (Cook et al., 2009; Yuan et al., 2010; Figure 1—figure supplement 1c, green box).
evidence: Determined by phylogenetic tree construction and multiple sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Total H2AX protein levels are increased during axolotl limb regeneration at 14 dpa.
source: We again found that the total amount of H2AX protein was increased during regeneration (Figure 1g), following the same trend as its mRNA levels (h2afx, Figure 1b and Figure 1e).
evidence: Shown by western blot analysis and corroborated by mRNA expression data.

claim: The relative ratio of γ-H2AX to total H2AX protein is decreased during axolotl limb regeneration at 14 dpa.
source: The total levels of γ-H2AX protein were also increased (Figure 1h); however, the relative ratio of γ-H2AX to total H2AX protein was decreased during regeneration (Figure 1i).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot quantification showing increased total γ-H2AX but decreased relative ratio.

claim: Relative pY142-H2AX levels are increased during axolotl limb regeneration at 14 dpa.
source: Interestingly, we identified that the relative pY142-H2AX levels were increased at 14 dpa (Figure 1j and Figure 1k), which suggested that H2AX regulation was important during regeneration and a potential target to study in association with DDR and genome integrity.
evidence: Shown by western blot analysis of phosphorylated H2AX forms.

claim: eya2 is the most highly-expressed gene of the Eya family during axolotl limb regeneration and is up-regulated post-amputation.
source: We found that eya2 is the most highly-expressed gene of its family and is also highly up-regulated post-amputation (Figure 2a, eya2) (Stewart et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on RNAseq data analysis and validated by qPCR.

claim: Genes involved in DNA repair and cell cycle are positively correlated with eya2 expression during limb regeneration.
source: Using this method, we found that the expression profiles of genes involved in DNA repair and cell cycle were positively correlated with eya2 expression, suggesting Eya2's involvement in these processes during limb regeneration (Figure 2d, blue bar).
evidence: Determined by co-expression correlation analysis and Gene Ontology Enrichment Analysis of RNAseq data.

claim: Axolotl Eya2 protein physically interacts with phosphorylated H2AX.
source: To test whether the axolotl Eya2 protein physically interacts with an H2AX-containing complex in cells, we performed an immunoprecipitation experiment using a tagged version of the axolotl Eya2, and we detected the phosphorylated form of H2AX in the precipitate (Figure 2e).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiment showing physical interaction.

claim: eya2 is expressed by most cells in the wound epidermis and blastema at 5 dpa.
source: To identify which cells express eya2 during regeneration, we performed RNA in situ hybridization and found eya2 mRNA detectable in the majority of blastema cells and wound epidermis at 5 dpa (red puncta, Figure 2f).
evidence: Shown by RNA in situ hybridization on tissue sections.

claim: eya2 and prrx1 co-localize in connective tissue progenitors throughout axolotl limb regeneration.
source: Indeed, time-course double in situ hybridization of eya2 and prrx1, a connective tissue progenitor marker (Gerber et al., 2018), further validated eya2 expression in the connective tissue lineage. We found that eya2 and prrx1 co-localized in connective tissue progenitors throughout regeneration, and we further observed eya2 expression in muscle as well.
evidence: Demonstrated by double in situ hybridization showing spatial co-expression patterns.

claim: eya2-/- axolotls have reduced blastema length compared to eya2+/- and eya2+/+ at multiple time points during regeneration.
source: The data indicated that eya2-/- axolotls have reduced blastema length compared to eya2+/- and eya2+/+ at multiple time points (Figure 3b and c).
evidence: Shown by quantitative measurements of blastema length over time with statistical significance.

claim: eya2-/- axolotls regenerate smaller limbs at 30 dpa compared to wild-type siblings.
source: To determine the size of the regenerate at 30 dpa, we measured their zeugopod length relative to animal size and found that eya2-/- animals regenerated smaller limbs, suggesting that the rate of regeneration was impaired (Figure 3e, see also Figure 3—figure supplement 2c–d for their size before amputation).
evidence: Demonstrated by skeletal staining and measurement of zeugopod length with statistical analysis.

claim: None of the eya2-/- animals had a fully-patterned skeleton at 30 dpa compared to 17% of eya2+/+ animals.
source: We then analyzed their skeletal pattern for completion and found that none of the eya2-/- animals (n = 0/18 limbs from nine animals) had a fully-patterned skeleton compared to 17% of eya2+/+ (n = 3/18 limbs from nine animals, 3 × 2 Contingency Table: p-value<0.05, Figure 3f).
evidence: Shown by skeletal pattern analysis with statistical significance.

claim: eya2-/- blastemas have fewer cells entering the cell cycle as measured by EdU incorporation.
source: Eya2-/- blastemas had reduced rates of cell cycle entry indicated by a decrease in EdU+ cells (Figure 3i) and decreased mitotic activity as evidenced by a decrease in pH3+ blastema cells (Figure 3j).
evidence: Demonstrated by EdU pulse-chase experiment and immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: eya2-/- blastemas have reduced mitotic activity as measured by pH3+ cells.
source: Eya2-/- blastemas had reduced rates of cell cycle entry indicated by a decrease in EdU+ cells (Figure 3i) and decreased mitotic activity as evidenced by a decrease in pH3+ blastema cells (Figure 3j).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining for phospho-Histone H3 and quantification.

claim: Cell cycle progression is stalled at the G2/M phase in eya2-/- blastemas.
source: Interestingly, we found a reduced percentage of double EdU+/pH3+ cells in the eya2-/- blastemas, which indicated that cell cycle progression was also stalled at the G2/M phase (Figure 3k).
evidence: Shown by quantification of double-positive EdU+/pH3+ cells indicating cells that entered S-phase but failed to complete mitosis.

claim: CDK2 levels are reduced in 5 dpa eya2-/- blastemas.
source: We found that the amount of the Cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2) was reduced in the 5 dpa eya2-/- blastemas whereas the G2/M-specific Cyclin B1 was increased (CCNB1, Figure 3—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis of cell cycle regulators.

claim: Cyclin B1 protein levels are increased in 5 dpa eya2-/- blastemas.
source: We found that the amount of the Cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2) was reduced in the 5 dpa eya2-/- blastemas whereas the G2/M-specific Cyclin B1 was increased (CCNB1, Figure 3—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis of cell cycle regulators.

claim: 5 dpa blastemas from eya2-/- animals have increased levels of relative γ-H2AX compared to eya2+/+ siblings.
source: We found that 5 dpa blastemas from eya2-/- animals had increased levels of relative γ-H2AX compared to those from eya2+/+ siblings (Figure 4b), suggesting that the activated cell cycle checkpoints may be associated with increased levels of genotoxic stress.
evidence: Shown by western blot analysis and quantification of γ-H2AX relative to total H2AX.

claim: eya2+/- blastemas show increased levels of pY142-H2AX.
source: In contrast, eya2+/- blastemas showed increased levels of pY142-H2AX, an outcome that correlated with the reduced Eya2 activity in the heterozygous background (Figure 4c and d).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis showing phosphorylation status of H2AX at Y142.

claim: No apoptotic cells are detected in eya2-/- blastemas by TUNEL staining.
source: This possibility is supported by TUNEL staining in which we could not detect blastema cells undergoing apoptosis in eya2-/- animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Shown by TUNEL assay on tissue sections.

claim: EdU+ blastema cells have more γ-H2AX foci per nuclear area than EdU- cells, irrespective of genotype.
source: Our analysis revealed that EdU+ cells had more γ-H2AX foci per nuclear area than EdU- cells, irrespective of genotype (Figure 4h, Two-way ANOVA, Row factor p-value<0.0001, F(1,30) = 62.39, DF = 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence quantification of γ-H2AX foci in EdU+ and EdU- cells with statistical analysis.

claim: EdU+ eya2-/- blastema cells have significantly more γ-H2AX foci per area compared to eya2+/+ cells.
source: Notably, our data revealed that EdU+ eya2-/- blastema cells had significantly more γ-H2AX foci per area compared to those of eya2+/+ (Figure 4h).
evidence: Shown by quantification of γ-H2AX foci in EdU+ cells across genotypes with statistical significance.

claim: Ablation of Eya2's transactivation and phosphatase domains does not affect the amount of DNA damage in blastema cells.
source: Since eya2-/- blastema cells showed increased levels of the DNA damage marker γ-H2AX they might have also accumulated DNA damage. To test this, we performed comet assays on blastema cells from all three genotypes and found that ablation of Eya2's transactivation and phosphatase domains does not affect the amount of DNA damage; hence, this phenotype appears specific to how DDR is regulated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Demonstrated by comet assay showing no difference in DNA damage across genotypes.

claim: Cell cycle-related genes are down-regulated in eya2-/- blastema tissues, especially at 14 dpa.
source: Focusing on the expression of genes associated with cell cycle progression, we found them significantly down-regulated in eya2-/- tissues, especially at the late-bud blastema (14 dpa, Figure 5a).
evidence: Shown by RNAseq analysis of cell cycle regulators.

claim: DNA damage response genes are up-regulated in eya2-/- blastemas compared to eya2+/- and eya2+/+.
source: To test whether this was at least in part related to genotoxic stress, we analyzed the expression of genes associated with DDR and found that they were up-regulated in eya2-/- blastemas versus eya2+/- and eya2+/+ (Figure 5b and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAseq analysis of DDR-related genes.

claim: eya2 expression is significantly up-regulated in eya2-/- tissues while other eya family members remain unchanged.
source: We found the expression of eya2 itself to be significantly up-regulated in the eya2-/- tissues, while the rest of the eya family remained unchanged, revealing a potential feedback loop specific to eya2 (Figure 5c).
evidence: Shown by RNAseq analysis of eya gene family expression.

claim: Genes known to regulate H2AX post-translational modifications are down-regulated in eya2-/- blastema tissues.
source: Genes known to regulate H2AX post-translational modifications were found down-regulated which indicated a potential negative feedback loop that could ameliorate the elevated γ-H2AX levels and dampen its effects (Figure 5d).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAseq analysis of H2AX regulators.

claim: The majority of genes involved in G1/S and G2/M transitions are down-regulated in eya2-/- blastemas.
source: The data showed that eya2-/- blastemas have down-regulated the majority of these genes, further strengthening our hypothesis that the cell cycle is stalled at the G1/S and G2/M checkpoints in absence of Eya2 activity (Figure 5f and g).
evidence: Shown by volcano plot analysis of cell cycle checkpoint genes from RNAseq data.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of Eya2 with MLS000544460 significantly reduces blastema length at 8 dpa.
source: As expected, Eya2 inhibition significantly reduced blastema length compared to DMSO controls at 8 dpa (Figure 6b and c).
evidence: Demonstrated by treatment with Eya2 inhibitor and measurement of blastema length.

claim: Eya2 inhibition decreases EdU+ cells in blastema following an 18 hr pulse.
source: This effect was accompanied by a decrease in EdU+ cells following an 18 hr pulse (Figure 6d and e) and an increase in TUNEL+ apoptotic cells (Figure 6d and f) in the treated limbs.
evidence: Shown by EdU incorporation assay and immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: Eya2 inhibition increases TUNEL+ apoptotic cells in blastema.
source: This effect was accompanied by a decrease in EdU+ cells following an 18 hr pulse (Figure 6d and e) and an increase in TUNEL+ apoptotic cells (Figure 6d and f) in the treated limbs.
evidence: Demonstrated by TUNEL assay and quantification.

claim: MLS000544460-treated blastema cells show increased levels of pY142-H2AX.
source: To corroborate these data, we used western blot analysis of H2AX where we detected increased levels of pY142- while γ-H2AX remained in the baseline (Figure 6g and h, Figure 6—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: Shown by western blot analysis of H2AX phosphorylation status.

claim: Eya2 inhibitor-treated blastema cells have more DNA damage than DMSO-treated controls.
source: To determine whether increased levels of DNA damage were also present in MLS000544460-treated blastema cells, we performed alkaline comet assays. We found more DNA damage present in blastema cells that had Eya2 activity blocked (Figure 6i), indicating that Eya2 is required for proper DDR in this context.
evidence: Demonstrated by comet assay showing increased DNA damage in treated cells.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of Chk1 and Chk2 reduces blastema length at 10 dpa.
source: Our data phenocopy the Eya2 inhibition, showing smaller blastema length (Figure 6k and l), reduced levels of EdU+ cells and increased TUNEL+ cells (Figure 6m and n) indicating reduced cell cycle progression and increased apoptosis.
evidence: Shown by treatment with Chk1/2 inhibitor and measurement of blastema length.

claim: Chk1/2 inhibition reduces EdU+ cells and increases TUNEL+ cells in blastema.
source: Our data phenocopy the Eya2 inhibition, showing smaller blastema length (Figure 6k and l), reduced levels of EdU+ cells and increased TUNEL+ cells (Figure 6m and n) indicating reduced cell cycle progression and increased apoptosis.
evidence: Demonstrated by EdU incorporation and TUNEL assays with quantification.

claim: Chk1/2 inhibition reduces levels of CDK2, CCNB1, and p-CDC2 in blastema.
source: To validate that the inhibitor deregulated the G1/S and G2/M checkpoints as intended we blotted for CDK2, CCNB1 and p-CDC2, and found them reduced upon Chk1 and Chk2 inhibition (Figure 6o).
evidence: Shown by western blot analysis of cell cycle regulators.

claim: eya2-/- axolotls develop normal limbs with muscle, bone, and nerves.
source: Eya2-/- axolotls developed normal limbs with muscle, bone, and nerves (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–d).
evidence: Demonstrated by histological analysis and immunofluorescence staining of intact limbs.

claim: eya2-/- axolotls have malformed kidneys and intra-peritoneal edema.
source: The eya2-/- animals could be easily identified by the presence of an intra-peritoneal edema which was also correlated with malformed kidneys (Figure 3—figure supplement 2e, red box).
evidence: Shown by cross-sectional analysis of whole animals.

claim: Blastema cells that have entered the cell cycle require more γ-H2AX to rapidly correct replication errors during proliferation.
source: Overall, these data indicated that blastema cells may require more γ-H2AX to rapidly correct replication errors during proliferation but kept a low γ-H2AX/H2AX ratio to reduce potential genotoxic stress signals that could hinder cell cycle progression (Rogakou et al., 1998; Fernandez-Capetillo et al., 2004).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that EdU+ cells have more γ-H2AX foci but the tissue maintains low relative γ-H2AX/H2AX ratio, combined with cited literature on γ-H2AX function.

claim: Eya2 plays a role in dampening the DNA damage response in cells following DNA repair.
source: Our molecular and biochemical data, however, strongly suggest an additional role for Eya2: dampening the DDR in cells following DNA repair. This is especially evident since progenitor cells lacking functional Eya2 have persistent γ-H2AX levels in combination with slower cell cycle dynamics without changes in DNA damage (Figure 4h, Figure 4—figure supplement 1e; Tu et al., 2013).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that eya2-/- cells have elevated γ-H2AX without increased DNA damage, suggesting a role in resolving DDR signaling.

claim: Genetic compensation occurs in eya2-/- axolotls through up-regulation of eya2 itself and other DDR genes.
source: Thus, our model is explained by the combination of a genetic compensation through mRNA degradation and feedback loops which up-regulated eya2 (Figure 5c) and mRNA surveillance mechanisms (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c) as well as functional compensation by up-regulation of DDR genes (Figure 5b) to facilitate the loss of Eya2 activity.
evidence: Inferred from RNAseq data showing up-regulation of eya2 and DDR genes in eya2-/- tissues, combined with the observation that these animals can still regenerate.

claim: The compensatory mechanism in eya2-/- axolotls may be established during early development.
source: We speculate that this compensatory mechanism is acquired during early phases of animal development since without it eya2-/- axolotls might be embryonic lethal as many dividing cells would trigger apoptosis.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observation that eya2-/- animals survive to adulthood despite lacking functional Eya2.

claim: The increased presence of γ-H2AX foci in eya2-/- EdU+ cells is due to more cells having a high number of foci per area.
source: We further identified that the increased presence of γ-H2AX foci was due to more cells having a high number of foci per area and fewer cells having low number of foci (Figure 4i).
evidence: Shown by distribution analysis of γ-H2AX foci concentrations in EdU+ cells.

claim: Differences in γ-H2AX foci per area in EdU+ cells are not due to variations in cell size.
source: We also found that EdU+ cells were bigger in size compared to EdU- cells across all genotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b, two-way ANOVA, Row Factor p-value=0.004, F(1,30)=16.13, DF = 1); however, differences in the number of γ-H2AX foci per area of the nucleus within the EdU+ population were not due to variations in the cell size (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b–c).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of cell size and γ-H2AX foci with statistical analysis showing no correlation.

claim: The effect of increased γ-H2AX foci is specific to cycling blastema cells.
source: In addition, when foci from all blastema cells were taken into consideration, there was no difference across genotypes; thus, the effect was found to be specific to cycling blastema cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Shown by comparison of γ-H2AX foci in all cells versus EdU+ cells only.

claim: Genes associated with metabolic processes and translation are over-represented in the dataset of genes down-regulated in eya2-/- tissues.
source: The most over-represented terms were genes associated with metabolic processes and translation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b, yellow and green nodes and Supplementary file 3), which previous studies have implicated as a sign of stress (Paschen et al., 2007; Liu and Qian, 2014; Lindqvist et al., 2018).
evidence: Shown by network analysis of RNAseq data with Gene Ontology enrichment.

claim: Genes associated with regulation of biological quality are over-represented in the dataset of genes up-regulated in eya2-/- tissues.
source: On the other hand, the most over-represented terms on the dataset with genes up-regulated in eya2-/- tissues were regulation of biological quality, a GO term that encapsulates genes related to driving cellular function to homeostasis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c, red nodes and Supplementary file 3) which may be part of a mechanism that compensates for the loss of Eya2 to alleviate the elevated DDR and stress.
evidence: Shown by network analysis of RNAseq data with Gene Ontology enrichment and interpretation.

claim: There is no loss of specific cell populations in eya2-/- blastemas based on marker gene expression.
source: Genes that define macrophages (APOE), wound epidermis (K1C12) and fibroblasts (DPT, LUM, PRRX1) were not found differentially expressed across genotypes, with the exception of the fibroblast marker prrx1 that appeared up-regulated in the eya2-/- tissues (Figure 5e). These data indicated that there was no loss of any particular cell type in the blastema in absence of Eya2 which further supported a broader role in DDR regulation and cell cycle progression for all limb progenitors.
evidence: Shown by RNAseq analysis of cell-type specific marker genes.

claim: The axolotl Eya2 protein structure is similar to human Eya2 and contains the three helices important for MLS000544460-mediated inhibition.
source: We first validated by protein structure analysis that axolotl Eya2 was similar to human Eya2 and displayed the three helices previously found to be important for MLS000544460-mediated inhibition (Krueger et al., 2014; Figure 6—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: Demonstrated by computational protein structure modeling and comparison.

claim: Different phenotypes between eya2-/- axolotls and Eya2 inhibitor-treated axolotls reveal functional compensation in the genetic mutants.
source: In addition, the different phenotypes observed between eya2-/- axolotls and Eya2 inhibitor-treated axolotls during regeneration, especially the increase in apoptotic cells in the latter, revealed that there is functional compensation that could prevent apoptosis in cells subject to genotoxic stress. This phenomenon has also been observed in other CRISPR/Cas9-mediated models including axolotls (Junker, 2019; Rossi et al., 2015; Tsai et al., 2020).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of phenotypes between genetic and pharmacological approaches, supported by literature on genetic compensation.

claim: Proper regulation of DNA damage response through Chk1 and Chk2 is important for tissue regeneration.
source: Taken together, by inhibiting another key aspect of DDR, we were able to impede tissue regrowth, further strengthening the hypothesis that proper regulation of genotoxic stress is required for regeneration.
evidence: Demonstrated by pharmacological inhibition of Chk1/2 showing impaired regeneration.

claim: DNA damage response is an innate part of the regeneration process in axolotls.
source: This study reveals that DDR is an innate part of the regeneration process and identifies Eya2 as a regulator of DDR and cell cycle progression during progenitor cell proliferation.
evidence: Concluded from multiple lines of evidence including transcriptomic analysis, genetic ablation, and pharmacological inhibition experiments.

claim: Eya2 regulates H2AX phosphorylation status and mediates cell cycle progression during limb regeneration.
source: Together, our data indicate that highly-regenerative animals employ a robust DNA damage response pathway which involves regulation of H2AX phosphorylation via Eya2 to facilitate proper cell cycle progression upon injury.
evidence: Concluded from genetic, biochemical, and pharmacological evidence showing Eya2's role in H2AX regulation and cell cycle control.

claim: Reduced p53 activity during early regeneration allows for progenitor cell cycle re-entry.
source: Previous studies have shown that during early phases of regeneration, the activity of p53 is reduced to allow for progenitor cell cycle re-entry (Yun et al., 2013), but it is later activated to enable differentiation (Villiard et al., 2007).
evidence: Based on cited previous studies.

claim: DNA damage is more likely to occur in non-coding regions like retrotransposons in amphibian genomes.
source: Their massive genome could also facilitate this process; it has been previously shown that DNA damage is more likely to occur in areas that do not encompass coding regions and regulatory elements, like retrotransposons, which are significantly abundant in amphibian genomes (Poetsch et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2019; Nowoshilow et al., 2018; Elewa et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on cited previous studies on DNA damage patterns and genome composition.

claim: High-throughput gene expression datasets show up-regulation of DNA repair genes across multiple organs and animal species during regeneration.
source: In addition, high-throughput gene expression datasets acquired from regenerative tissues show up-regulation of DNA repair genes across multiple organs and animal species, indicating that a proper DDR might be an innate part of the regenerative mechanism (Sousounis et al., 2014; Darnet et al., 2019; Barghouth et al., 2019; Shiroor et al., 2019; Bedelbaeva et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on cited studies showing consistent patterns across different regenerative contexts.

claim: Senescent cells are cleared from regenerating tissues in amphibians.
source: This mechanism could occur in conjunction with clearing senescent cells from regenerating tissues, which would allow only resilient proliferating progenitors to be present in the blastema (Yun et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on cited study on senescent cell clearance during regeneration.

claim: Eya2 is considered a biomarker for certain cancers.
source: Interestingly, Eya2 is also considered a biomarker for certain cancers, indicating that many more types of proliferating cells may up-regulate eya2 (Fu et al., 2014; Yuan et al., 2016; Wen et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on cited studies on Eya2 expression in cancer.

claim: Eya2 prevents apoptosis by dephosphorylating pY142-H2AX which promotes DNA repair.
source: Based on its most documented function during DDR, Eya2 prevents apoptosis by dephosphorylating pY142-H2AX which subsequently promotes DNA repair (Cook et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on cited study on Eya2 function in DDR.

claim: Cancer cells might utilize Eya2 to bypass proper genotoxic stress signaling and promote rapid cell cycle entry.
source: It is interesting to speculate that cancer cells might utilize Eya2 to bypass proper genotoxic stress signaling, preventing DDR initiation and thereby promoting rapid cell cycle entry, in addition to its already documented role in cell invasion (Wen et al., 2017).
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observed role of Eya2 in dampening DDR and its association with cancer.

claim: Eya proteins act as transcriptional co-activators in other systems.
source: As Eya proteins have been shown to act as transcriptional co-activators in other systems, considering a possible co-activation role for Eya2 in axolotl limb regeneration will also be important and the subject of future study (Jemc and Rebay, 2007).
evidence: Based on cited study on Eya protein function.
